title: Choose Math World's visual world
question: The roll assigned The Build Booklet. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Build Booklet
options.lineage: wordless toy-construction instruction booklets (exploded isometric steps, '2x' part callouts)
options.thesis: Math World as a wordless build manual. Every screen is a numbered step, and every quantity is a parts callout. '5× [row of 8]' is multiplication written the way a builder already reads it.
materials: flat 3-tone isometric parts with ink outlines
options.viewport: The Resting Bay is the booklet's current step page. A giant step number and the next mission's sub-assembly (the planet fleet drawn as an exploded parts callout, e.g. '7× ▢▢▢▢▢▢▢▢') lead, with the Launch action as the finished-model arrow. The Hangar, Academy and Map sit as three sub-assembly callout boxes along the side. The times-table wall is the parts inventory page at the back, shown only as a folded tab until opened.
options.risk: It can tip into toy-manual literalism and lose the space adventure if the parts are not rockets, drones and planets. It also must avoid any toy brand's marks.

raised.raise: Route changes are page turns of one continuous booklet, never hard cuts between unrelated screens.
History stays visible: the previous step's result sits in the corner, the way a manual shows the last build.
The bay is drawn as one continuous cutaway section of the ship, so every room has a real place in it.
Mastery states are labelled by shape (empty outline, dashed, filled, starred), not colour alone.

options.label: Isotype Squadrons
options.lineage: Otto Neurath and Gerd Arntz's Isotype pictorial statistics (Vienna, 1920s-30s)
options.thesis: Count, don't read. Every quantity is a row of identical pictograms, so a fleet of 6 squads × 8 is literally an Isotype chart you shoot at, and mastery is a chart that fills in.
materials: flat pictograms on an unprinted ground
options.viewport: The Resting Bay as a single Isotype plate. The next mission is a big pictogram row block with one line of plain caption and the Launch action under it. Three small plates (Hangar, Academy, Map) sit in the same grammar. The times-table wall is a 10×10 field of tiny glyphs that fill as facts turn Gold.
options.risk: It is my top grounded candidate and familiar to anyone who knows infographic history. It can read cool and museum-like for an eight-year-old unless the pictograms have character.

options.label: Teletext Service
options.thesis: Keying digits is the whole input, as in the battle. Every screen is a three-digit page, and hidden answers wait behind REVEAL, which maps directly onto the hint ladder.
materials: one bitmap face in a 40×24 grid
options.viewport: P100 RESTING BAY: the next mission as a double-height header with a mosaic planet, routes as page numbers (P200 MAP, P300 HANGAR, P400 ACADEMY), and the times tables behind REVEAL.
options.case: Holds product clarity (digits as input, REVEAL as the hint ladder), but kids outside the UK and Europe will not recognise it.
options.risk: Retro novelty if the grid is not strict; very low-resolution art for a game.

options.label: Crouwel Grid Specimen
options.thesis: Multiplication is an array. Every number, fleet and wall cell is built cell by cell on a visible construction grid, so 7 × 8 is drawn as the grid that makes 56.
options.viewport: The next mission's numerals built huge from grid cells across the bay, with the Launch action on the accent plane and the routes as small grid-set labels.
options.case: Holds product clarity (arrays are multiplication), but audience identification is weak for kids.
options.risk: Austere: a design poster rather than a place to come home to.

options.label: Shader Portal
options.case: Fuses poorly: it hides the next action behind atmosphere, and kids don't read thin corner links.
options.kept: One continuous transition between screens instead of DOM swaps.

options.label: Torn Flyer Wall
options.case: Fuses poorly: the club-night register suits neither kids nor a maths tutor.
options.kept: Past states stay visible as layers.

options.label: Daylight Section
options.case: Fuses poorly: lovely, but nothing in it carries counting or mastery.
options.kept: One continuous cutaway that gives every room a real place.

options.label: Accretion Disk
options.case: Fuses poorly: it is the dark sci-fi neon look the game has now.
options.kept: A named state vocabulary that does not rely on colour.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A bright illustrated kids'-game hub like the big maths RPGs: a painted scene, a waving mascot, big rounded buttons, a currency counter.
canonCard.viewport: A cheerful illustrated room with the mascot centre-left and three big buttons.
canonCard.risk: This is the generic kids-edtech look you named as wrong, done well.
